hints: Look carefully at Fig. 2.1 and compare the six chromosomes for overall length and thickness and the dark and light stained bands - which two look like matching copies?
walkthrough:
What Makes Chromosomes Homologous**
Homologous means the two chromosomes are the same type. They came one from each parent, so they have the same length, the centromere in the same position giving the same shape, and the same pattern of stained bands.

Picking The Pair in Fig. 2.1**
Scan the six chromosomes and find the two that are identical twins in appearance. Circle just those two. You do not need to name them, the visual match of size and banding is the identification.
Final answer: Circle two chromosomes that match in size, shape and banding pattern (one homologous pair).

hints: Start with what you can actually see in Fig. 2.2 - compare the two chromosome 11 structures side by side for length and overall outline.
Now think beyond appearance to what the identical banding tells you about DNA content - what is carried at the same positions on both?
Finish by linking structure to behaviour - what do homologous chromosomes do together in prophase I of meiosis?
walkthrough:
Same Physical Appearance**
The two chromosomes in Fig. 2.2 have the same length and the same shape, with the centromere in the same place. That is the first clue they are the same chromosome type, one maternal and one paternal.

Same Internal Organisation**
Staining gives the identical pattern of dark and light bands along both. Bands reflect DNA sequence, so identical banding means the same number of base pairs and the same genes in the same order at the same loci. Alleles may differ, but loci do not.

Same Meiotic Behaviour**
Because they carry the same loci, they can pair up precisely in prophase I of meiosis to form a bivalent. That pairing ability is part of the definition of homologous.
Final answer: Same size / length / number of base pairs; same shape / centromere position; same banding pattern; same order of genes / loci; pair up to form a bivalent in prophase I.

hints: Remember spermatozoa are gametes, so think about how the chromosome number in a gamete relates to the diploid number of 40 given for the mouse.
walkthrough:
Halving The Diploid Number**
Body cells are diploid, $2n = 40$, with two of each homologous chromosome. Gametes are haploid, $n$, with only one of each pair after meiosis. So $n = 40 \div 2 = 20$ chromosomes in a spermatozoon.
Final answer: $40 \div 2 = 20$ chromosomes.

hints: Focus on what happens to chromosome number during meiosis compared with mitosis - what does the term reduction division mean?
Now follow what happens next at fertilisation when two gametes fuse - why must gametes start with half the number?
walkthrough:
Halving The Number**
Meiosis is a reduction division. A diploid cell with 40 chromosomes produces haploid gametes with 20 chromosomes. Only one homologue of each pair goes into each gamete.

Restoring The Number At Fertilisation**
At fertilisation two haploid nuclei fuse, $20 + 20 = 40$. This restores the diploid $2n$ number in the zygote. Without the halving step, fusion would double the number every generation, $40$ to $80$ to $160$.

Final answer: Meiosis is a reduction division that halves the chromosome number to haploid; fertilisation / fusion of gametes then restores the diploid number / $2n$ / 40 and prevents doubling each generation.

hints: Think about what a recessive allele needs in order to be seen in the phenotype - can one copy alone have an effect when a dominant allele is present?
Now imagine millions of genetically different sperm and eggs fusing at random - how could two rare copies end up together in one zygote?
walkthrough:
Recessive Means Two Copies Needed**
A recessive allele is only expressed when no dominant allele masks it. The offspring must inherit the recessive allele from both parents.

Random Fusion Brings Them Together**
Because fusion is random, there is a small chance that a sperm carrying the rare recessive allele meets an egg carrying the same rare recessive allele. The resulting zygote has a pair of recessive alleles, a homozygous recessive genotype, and so shows the trait.
Final answer: By chance both fusing gametes may each carry the recessive allele; the zygote then receives two copies and is homozygous recessive, so the recessive phenotype is expressed.

hints: Start with the effect of changing one base in DNA on the mRNA codon - what new type of codon could be created that does not specify an amino acid?
Then think about what the ribosome does when it reaches that codon during translation - what happens to the rest of the message downstream?
walkthrough:
Creating A Premature Stop Signal**
Changing one base can change an amino-acid-coding triplet into one of the STOP codons, $UAA$, $UAG$ or $UGA$ on mRNA. A STOP codon has no tRNA and codes for no amino acid.

Early Termination Of Translation**
When the ribosome reaches the premature STOP codon, translation terminates and the polypeptide is released. All codons after that point are never translated, so only a short fragment is made.

Final answer: Substitution creates a STOP codon which does not code for an amino acid; translation stops there so the rest of the mRNA / later codons are not translated, giving a very short polypeptide.

hints: Work out which allele must be dominant from the information - if both heterozygous parents look normal, what does that tell you about the woolly allele?
Write the two parental genotypes and then split each to show the two types of gametes each parent can make.
Combine the gametes systematically to list offspring genotypes and then translate each genotype into normal or woolly coat.
walkthrough:
Setting Parental Genotypes**
Normal is dominant to woolly because two normal-coated heterozygotes can produce woolly offspring. Let A = normal, a = woolly. Both parents are Aa. So: parental genotypes Aa x Aa.

Listing Gametes**
By segregation each parent makes two gamete types in equal numbers: gametes A and a from the father, and A and a from the mother.

Predicting Offspring**
Random fusion gives: offspring genotypes AA, Aa, Aa, aa in a 1:2:1 ratio. AA and Aa contain the dominant A so are normal coat; only aa lacks A so is woolly coat. Offspring phenotypes: 3 normal : 1 woolly.

Final answer: parental genotypes: Aa x Aa; gametes: A, a and A, a; offspring genotypes: AA, Aa, Aa, aa; offspring phenotypes: normal, normal, normal, woolly (3 normal : 1 woolly). Woolly is recessive.
